section.heading: 2.9 Dimension and Rank
section.paragraph: This section continues the discussion of subspaces and bases for subspaces, beginning with the concept of a coordinate system. The definition and example below should make a useful new term, dimension, seem quite natural, at least for subspaces of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ .﻿
section.heading: Coordinate Systems
section.paragraph: The main reason for selecting a basis for a subspace $$H$$ , instead of merely a spanning set, is that each vector in $$H$$ can be written in only one way as a linear combination of the basis vectors. To see why, suppose $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{p}\}$$ is a basis for $$H$$ , and suppose a vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$H$$ can be generated in two ways, say,
Since $$B$$ is linearly independent, the weights in (2) must all be zero. That is, $$c_{j} = d_{j}$$ for $$1 \leq j \leq p,$$ which shows that the two representations in (1) are actually the same.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Suppose the set $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{p}\}$$ is a basis for a subspace $$H$$ . For each $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$H,$$ the coordinates of $$\mathbf{x}$$ relative to the basis $$B$$ are the weights $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ such that $$\textbf{x} = c_{1}\textbf{b}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{b}_{p},$$ and the vector in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$
is called the coordinate vector of $$x$$ (relative to $$B$$ ) or the $$B - \text{coordinate}$$ vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ .1

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 12 \\ 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$B = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ . Then $$B$$ is a basis for $$H = \text{Span} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ because $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ are linearly independent. Determine if $$\textbf{x}$$ is in $$H$$ , and if it is, find the coordinate vector of $$\textbf{x}$$ relative to $$B$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Notice that although points in $$H$$ are also in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , they are completely determined by their coordinate vectors, which belong to $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . The grid on the plane in Figure 1 makes $$H$$ “look” like $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . The correspondence $$\textbf{x}\mapsto\begin{bmatrix} \textbf{x} \end{bmatrix}_{B}$$ is a one-to-one correspondence between $$H$$ and $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ that preserves linear combinations. We call such a correspondence an isomorphism, and we say that $$H$$ is isomorphic to $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ .﻿

In general, if $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{p}\}$$ is a basis for $$H$$ , then the mapping $$\textbf{x}\mapsto\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$$ is a one-to-one correspondence that makes $$H$$ look and act the same as $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ (even though the vectors in $$H$$ themselves may have more than $$p$$ entries). (Section 4.4 has more details.)
section.heading: The Dimension of a Subspace
section.paragraph: It can be shown that if a subspace $$H$$ has a basis of $$p$$ vectors, then every basis of $$H$$ must consist of exactly $$p$$ vectors. (See Exercises 35 and 36.) Thus the following definition makes sense.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The dimension of a nonzero subspace $$H$$ , denoted by $$\text{dim} H$$ , is the number of vectors in any basis for $$H$$ The dimension of the zero subspace $$\{\textbf{0}\}$$ is defined to be zero.2

section.paragraph: The space $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ has dimension $$n$$ . Every basis for $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ consists of $$n$$ vectors. A plane through $$\textbf{0}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ is two-dimensional, and a line through $$\textbf{0}$$ is one-dimensional.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Recall that the null space of the matrix $$A$$ in Example 6 in Section 2.8 had a basis of $$3$$ vectors. So the dimension of $$\text{Nul} A$$ in this case is $$3$$ . Observe how each basis vector corresponds to a free variable in the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ . Our construction always produces a basis in this way. So, to find the dimension of $$\text{Nul} A$$ , simply identify and count the number of free variables in $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ .﻿

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The rank of a matrix $$A$$ , denoted by $$\text{rank} A$$ , is the dimension of the column space of $$A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Since the pivot columns of $$A$$ form a basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ , the rank of $$A$$ is just the number of pivot columns in $$A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The row reduction in Example 3 reveals that there are two free variables in $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , because two of the five columns of $$A$$ are not pivot columns. (The nonpivot columns correspond to the free variables in $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ .) Since the number of pivot columns plus the number of nonpivot columns is exactly the number of columns, the dimensions of $$\text{Col} A$$ and $$\text{Nul} A$$ have the following useful connection. (See the Rank Theorem in Section 4.6 for additional details.)

note.title: Theorem 14
note.heading: Theorem 14
The Rank Theorem
note.paragraph: If a matrix $$A$$ has $$n$$ columns, then $$\text{rank} A + \dim \text{Nul} A = n$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The following theorem is important for applications and will be needed in Chapters 5 and 6. The theorem (proved in Section 4.5) is certainly plausible, if you think of a $$p$$ -dimensional subspace as isomorphic to $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ . The Invertible Matrix Theorem shows that $$p$$ vectors in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ are linearly independent if and only if they also span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$$ .﻿

note.title: Theorem 15
note.heading: Theorem 15
The Basis Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$H$$ be a $$p$$ -dimensional subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}.$$ Any linearly independent set of exactly $$p$$ elements in $$H$$ is automatically a basis for $$H.$$ Also, any set of $$p$$ elements of $$H$$ that spans $$H$$ is automatically a basis for $$H .$$

section.heading: Rank and the Invertible Matrix Theorem
section.paragraph: The various vector space concepts associated with a matrix provide several more statements for the Invertible Matrix Theorem. They are presented below to follow the statements in the original theorem in Section 2.3.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
The Invertible Matrix Theorem (continued)
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix. Then the following statements are each equivalent to the statement that $$A$$ is an invertible matrix.

list.item: The columns of $$A$$ form a basis of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n} .$$

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Statement $$(m)$$ is logically equivalent to statements $$(e)$$ and $$(h)$$ regarding linear independence and spanning. The other four statements are linked to the earlier ones of the theorem by the following chain of almost trivial implications:

$$\left(\right. g \left.\right) \Rightarrow \left(\right. n \left.\right) \Rightarrow \left(\right. o \left.\right) \Rightarrow \left(\right. p \left.\right) \Rightarrow \left(\right. q \left.\right) \Rightarrow \left(\right. d \left.\right)$$

Statement $$(g)$$ , which says that the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has at least one solution for each $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , implies statement $$(n)$$ , because $$\text{Col} A$$ is precisely the set of all $$\textbf{b}$$ such that the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is consistent. The implications $$\left(\right. n \left.\right)$$ $$\Rightarrow$$ $$\left(\right. o \left.\right)$$ $$\Rightarrow$$ $$(p)$$ follow from the definitions of dimension and rank. If the rank of $$A$$ is $$n,$$ the number of columns of $$A$$ , then $$\text{dim Nul} A = 0$$ , by the Rank Theorem, and so $$\text{Nul} A = \{\textbf{0}\}$$ . Thus $$\left(\right. p \left.\right)$$ $$\Rightarrow$$ $$(q)$$ . Also, statement $$(q)$$ implies that the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has only the trivial solution, which is statement $$(d)$$ . Since statements $$(d)$$ and $$(g)$$ are already known to be equivalent to the statement that $$A$$ is invertible, the proof is complete.

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: Many algorithms discussed in this text are useful for understanding concepts and making simple computations by hand. However, the algorithms are often unsuitable for large-scale problems in real life.

Rank determination is a good example. It would seem easy to reduce a matrix to echelon form and count the pivots. But unless exact arithmetic is performed on a matrix whose entries are specified exactly, row operations can change the apparent rank of a matrix. For instance, if the value of $$x$$ in the matrix $$\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 7 \\ 5 & x \end{bmatrix}$$ is not stored exactly as $$7$$ in a computer, then the rank may be $$1$$ or $$2$$ , depending on whether the computer treats $$x - 7$$ as zero.
In practical applications, the effective rank of a matrix $$A$$ is often determined from the singular value decomposition of $$A,$$ to be discussed in Section 7.4.
